title: Why a gas pushes: pressure from collisions
summary: Gas pressure is the combined push of countless molecules hitting the walls.
alt: A cylinder of gas with a piston. Molecules bounce around; bars show the hits per second and the pressure.

gas.label: Gas molecules
gas.text: The molecules of the gas (colour = speed: blue slow, red fast).

me.label: Pressure
me.text: What the simulated gas shows right now.

shapes.text: Pressure = push of all the hits

steps.title: A gas is a swarm of molecules
steps.text: A gas is made of **huge numbers of tiny molecules** flying about in all directions. They are far apart and move in straight lines until they hit something. Colour shows speed: blue is slow, red is fast.

steps.title: Every hit is a tiny push
steps.text: When a molecule hits the piston it bounces back, so the piston gets a tiny **push**. Millions of hits every second blur into one steady force. **Force on each unit area is the pressure.** The bar below counts the hits: {{gh|1}} per second.

steps.title: More molecules, more hits
steps.text: Double the number of molecules (40 → 80). Twice as many hits means twice the push, so the pressure goes **up in proportion to N**.

steps.title: A hotter gas hits harder
steps.text: Back to 40 molecules; now heat the gas from 300 K to 600 K. Molecules move **faster**, so each hit is harder **and** hits come more often. Pressure rises.

steps.title: A smaller box means more hits
steps.text: Squeeze the gas into half the length. The molecules reach the piston twice as often, so the pressure **doubles**. Pressure goes as **1/V**.

steps.title: Pressure depends on N, T and V
steps.text: All three effects together: \( P \propto \dfrac{N\,T}{V} \). Now try it yourself: change the sliders and watch the hits per second and the pressure follow.

formulas.title: Pressure of a gas
formulas.text: More molecules or more heat raise the pressure; more room lowers it.

formulas.title: Kinetic theory result
formulas.text: N/V is the number of molecules per volume, m is the mass of one molecule, \( \overline{v^2} \) is the mean square speed.

challenges.title: Now you try
challenges.prompt: The gas shows **1 P₀**. You double the temperature (N and V stay the same). What is the pressure in units of P₀?
challenges.hint: Pressure is proportional to temperature (in kelvin).
challenges.explain: P ∝ T, so doubling T doubles P: **2 P₀**.

challenges.title: Now you try
challenges.prompt: Both the number of molecules **and** the volume are doubled (same temperature). What is the new pressure in P₀ (start at 1 P₀)?
challenges.hint: N doubles but V doubles too.
challenges.explain: P ∝ N/V: twice as many molecules in twice the room hit the walls just as often. Pressure stays **1 P₀**.

challenges.title: Now you try
challenges.prompt: Which change would **lower** the pressure of a gas in a closed cylinder?
challenges.hint: Lower pressure means fewer hits on the walls.
challenges.explain: A bigger volume means molecules reach the walls less often, so the pressure falls.

takeaways: Gas pressure is the **combined force of molecular hits** on the walls, per unit area.
More molecules, higher temperature or smaller volume all give **more (or harder) hits** and so more pressure.
The three together: \( P \propto NT/V \) — the idea behind every gas law.

notes.title: Connects to
notes.text: Next: **Boyle's law** (change V, keep T) and **Charles's law** (change T, keep P). All gas laws come from this one picture. Temperature itself is the average kinetic energy of the molecules.
